function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **ready‑to‑drop** set of files you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository, followed by the exact Git commands you’ll need to stage, commit and push them.

> **Assumptions**  
> * The repo contains a very small Express/Node.js app that listens on port **3000** (`app.js` or similar).  
> * No special build steps are required beyond `npm ci`.  
> * You want the Docker image pushed to the GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) so it can be referenced from the Kubernetes manifests.

---

## 1️⃣ Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js 18 image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install only production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Alpine gives a small footprint.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> * The container will listen on port 3000 – the same port the app uses locally.

---

## 2️⃣ Kubernetes Manifests

Create a directory called `k8s` (or `deployments`) and add a file named `nodejs-welcome.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port exposed inside the cluster
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80 (internally forwards to 3000).  
> * Uses the image that will be built/pushed by the GitHub Actions workflow.

---

## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t already exist) and add a file named `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Key points**  
> * The workflow triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * It builds the Docker image and tags it with the commit SHA.  
> * It pushes the image to GHCR using the automatically generated `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> * No manual secrets are required – the token is available by default.

---

## 4️⃣ Git Commands

Open a terminal, navigate to the cloned repo, then run:

```bash
# Stage the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/nodejs-welcome.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit with a clear message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote `main` branch
git push origin main
```

> If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

### 🎉 Done!

After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the Docker image, and push it to GHCR. Your Kubernetes manifests reference that image, so you can deploy to any cluster that has access to GHCR (or you can change the image tag to `latest` once you’re ready).

Feel free to tweak the replica count, service type, or Node.js version as your project evolves. Happy coding!
